content: The existing evidence regarding the implementation of Option B+ highlights significant challenges in ensuring adherence to and retention in care among pregnant and postpartum women. These challenges are particularly pronounced during the postpartum period. One of the key issues is the rapid initiation of antiretroviral therapy (ART), often on the same day as diagnosis, which may overwhelm patients and hinder their ability to fully comprehend and accept the lifelong nature of the treatment. This same-day start approach may contribute to difficulties in adherence, as it can be perceived as too much, too soon. To address these challenges, it is essential to provide enhanced education and counseling to pregnant women, emphasizing the maternal health benefits of Option B+ and fostering greater patient acceptance. This support should also help women come to terms with the necessity of lifelong ART. Additionally, community-based or peer support systems could play a critical role in improving retention, particularly for adolescent mothers, who are at a higher risk of being lost to follow-up compared to older women. The World Health Organization (WHO) strongly recommends initiating ART for all pregnant and breastfeeding women living with HIV, regardless of their clinical stage or CD4 cell count, and continuing treatment for life. This recommendation is based on moderate-quality evidence and aims to prevent mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT) of HIV while improving maternal health outcomes. Research priorities include conducting randomized controlled trials to compare the effectiveness of Option B and Option B+, as well as implementation research to evaluate the real-world effectiveness of Option B+. Studies should also explore the benefits of integrating ART services within maternal, newborn, and child health services versus referring women to separate ART programs. Determining the optimal timing for referrals after delivery is another critical area of investigation. Several studies have documented the challenges and outcomes associated with Option B+ implementation. For example, research in Malawi and Kenya has shown that loss to follow-up and poor adherence are common issues, particularly among adolescent mothers. Factors such as unintended pregnancies, poor birth outcomes, and limited postpartum contraceptive use further complicate the situation. Studies have also highlighted the importance of addressing maternal CD4 cell count decline after ART interruption and the emergence of drug resistance in some cases. In summary, while Option B+ offers significant benefits for PMTCT and maternal health, its successful implementation requires addressing barriers to adherence and retention through targeted education, counseling, and support systems. Further research is needed to optimize strategies for integrating ART services and improving outcomes for both mothers and their infants.
